questions.0.question.back: What happened in Singapore on 15 February 1942?
questions.0.question.source: What happened in Singapore on 15 February 1942?

questions.0.options.0.text.source: The occupation came to an end.

questions.0.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. The occupation ended in 1945. On 15 February 1942, the occupation began. Look at Lesson 7 again.
questions.0.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The occupation ended in 1945. On 15 February 1942, it began. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.0.options.1.text.back: Japanese-language lessons at school were stopped.

questions.0.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. In 1942, Japanese-language lessons became compulsory at school. Look at Lesson 7 again.
questions.0.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. In 1942, Japanese lessons became compulsory in schools. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.0.options.2.feedback.back: Yes. British forces surrendered at the Ford Factory. Then the occupation began. The occupation lasted until 1945.
questions.0.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. British forces gave up at the Ford Factory. Then the occupation began. It lasted until 1945.

questions.1.question.back: You want to know what people in Singapore ate in 1943. Which source helps most?
questions.1.question.source: You want to learn what people in Singapore ate in 1943. Which source would help most?

questions.1.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. Lee Geok Boi used oral history interviews to write about food in this time. Memories can tell about everyday meals.
questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Lee Geok Boi used oral history interviews to write about food in this time. Memories can tell us about meals.

questions.1.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. That photo shows the building in 2025. That photo cannot show what people ate in 1943. Look at Lesson 7 again.

questions.1.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. That rule tells about lessons at school, not about food. Look at Lesson 7 again.

questions.2.question.back: On 17 August 1945, two leaders declared in public that Indonesia was free. What is the name of a statement like this?
questions.2.question.source: On 17 August 1945, two leaders said in public that Indonesia was free. What is this kind of statement called?

questions.2.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. A proclamation is a statement for everyone. In Indonesia, people commemorate 17 August as the day they became free.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. A proclamation is a statement made to all. In Indonesia, people mark 17 August as the day they became free.

questions.2.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. The Netherlands handed over power later, in 1949. That happened after the proclamation. Look at Lesson 8 again.
questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The Netherlands handed over power later, in 1949. That came after the proclamation. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.2.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. A federation is a union of several states under one main government. Look at Lesson 8 again.
questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A federation is a group of states joined under one main government. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.3.question.back: A pupil says that Malaysia became free on 31 August 1957. What needs to be changed?
questions.3.question.source: A student says that Malaysia became free on 31 August 1957. What needs to change?

questions.3.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. 17 August 1945 is the date of Indonesia's proclamation. Look at Lesson 8 again.
questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. 17 August 1945 is the date of Indonesia's proclamation. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.3.options.1.text.back: Change Malaysia to the Federation of Malaya
questions.3.options.1.text.source: Change Malaysia to the Federation of Malaya

questions.3.options.1.feedback.back: Yes. It was the Federation of Malaya that became free in 1957. Malaysia was only formed later, in 1963.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. It was the Federation of Malaya that became free in 1957. Malaysia was formed later, in 1963.

questions.3.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. In 1956, the leaders signed an agreement in London. That agreement set independence day in 1957. Look at Lesson 8 again.
questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. In 1956, leaders signed an agreement in London. It set the day of independence in 1957. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.4.question.back: In March 2000, a UN report said many schools in Timor-Leste had been repaired. What does this date tell you?
questions.4.question.source: In March 2000, a UN report said many schools in Timor-Leste had been repaired. What does this date tell you?

questions.4.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. That report is from 2000. That is before independence was restored in 2002. Look at Lesson 9 again.
questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The report is from 2000. That is before independence was restored in 2002. Look back at Lesson 9.

questions.4.options.1.feedback.back: Yes. The work of repairing schools began before 2002, when a UN team ran the country together with East Timorese leaders.

questions.4.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. 2024 is the date of that school photo. Repairs began much earlier. Look at Lesson 9 again.
questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. 2024 is the date of the school photo. Repairs began much earlier. Look back at Lesson 9.
